title: Why the Moon always shows the same face (tidal locking)
sources: NASA Science: 'Tidal Locking' and Moon facts pages
Wikipedia 'Tidal locking' and 'Far side of the Moon'

verified.text: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth: it spins once on its own axis in the same time it takes to go once around Earth, about 27.3 days — so one spin equals one orbit.
Because the spin and the orbit take the same time, the same half of the Moon, the near side, always faces Earth.
Long ago the young Moon spun faster. Earth's gravity stretched it slightly, raising a bulge, and Earth's pull on that bulge slowly braked the Moon's spin until it matched its orbit.
The Moon's far side is not permanently dark: it gets as much sunlight as the near side, just at different times.
Because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted and oval, a small wobble called libration lets us see about 59 percent of its surface over time.
Many large moons are tidally locked to their planets, including Jupiter's four largest moons.
The far side of the Moon was first photographed by the Soviet Luna 3 probe in 1959.

knownErrors.text: The far side of the Moon is always dark
knownErrors.correction: The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side; it only always faces away from Earth.
The Moon does rotate, once per orbit, which is why the same side faces Earth.
